speakeroldname: Mr. T. F. DONNELLY (Willow Bunch) moved:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in seconding this resolution I desire to direct the attention of the house to two or three matters which have come to my attention since I spoke on this subject last year. After the matter had been brought to the attention of the house at the last session a reply, or an attempted reply, to the statements made was published in the Financial Post of June 18, 1931. In this article the oil companies endeavoured to

Price oj Gasoline-Mr. Bothwell
justify the prices which they were charging the public in Canada. I take exception to certain of the figures given in that article, and I believe that many hon. members will agree with me when I say that many of them do not represent the prices charged throughout Canada. For instance, in order to show that in the city of Toronto they were not charging a price greater than that which would permit them to make a reasonable profit, they show an allowance for tank wagon distribution of 4 cents per gallon and an allowance for service station distribution of 5 cents per gallon. I do not know the particular charges in different parts of Ontario, but from my knowledge of those districts on the prairies to which I have had access I can say that no such charges are allowed, and I cannot see how or why such a charge should be allowed in the city of Toronto. The tank wagon allowance runs from 1 to 2i cents instead of 4 cents, while the service station charge runs from 2 to 3 cents. In setting forth why they require protection they state:
There are several grounds on which the Canadian oil industry based its appeals for protection:
1.	That Canada's population of ten million people is scattered over an area greater than that of the United States, and that a large part of the thinly populated territory has to be serviced at a loss.
It will be found that the price of gasoline in different parts of Canada varies according to the district. If you travel away from the railroad you must pay several cents per gallon more than at points on the railway line. I doubt very much the truth of the statement that the people in any particular part of Canada are being serviced at a loss. That is one matter which the committee on banking and commerce could investigate.
The second reason given for the necessity of protection is:
2.	That because of the long winter Canadians demand and receive a much better quality of gasoline than is commonly thought necessary in most parts of the United States and that a large number of Canadian service stations outside the large cities lose money in the winter.
It may be true that some service stations lose money during the winter, as there are any number which are not financed by the oil companies and which close during that season. If the others are operating at a loss I imagine they would do so but a short time before they would be closed.
I have a good deal of doubt, too, about the next statement; in any event it could be investigated :
3.	That the refining capacity being developed in Canada and the immense sums being spent by such companies as Imperial Oil and British American Oil in the last year on modernizing plants create employment which is of prime national benefit.
Surely that is no reason at all why all the people of Canada who are users of gasoline should be exploited to the extent that the figures given by the hon. member for Willow Bunch would indicate. The next one reads:
4.	That since the protection was given the price of gasoline has been successively lowered to its present level, and that the industry could not do better than at present except at a loss, even if it received the crude petroleum for nothing, unless freight rates came down or taxes disappeared. Cost prices given in the tables are average prices. In a city better results can be obtained than in a place of smaller population.
Those are the four reasons which the oil companies allege as entitling them to protection.
The hon. member for Willow Bunch gave figures as to what we are paying for gasoline in excess of what he believes the ' proper price should be, allowing a reasonable profit. On the 30th of November of last year the Regina Leader-Post obtained by telegram information from fifteen United States cities as to the prices of gasoline, and I want to read to the house the results of their findings. On that date, November 30, 1931, the report showed:
The average price of white gas in Canadian cities was 31-37 cents, against a United States average of 24-21 cents, or a difference of 7-16 cents.
These figures are reached by taking into consideration various government taxes _ and also adjusting American prices to imperial gallon measure. Gasoline is sold south of the border on a basis of American gallon, smaller than the imperial gallon used in Canada.
Then they give the comparisons showing the average on the 30th of November last. The figures are as follows:
	White	Ethyl
	gas	gas
	cents	cents
Western Canada	.. 31-37	34-93United States cities..	.. 24-21	27-81Difference	.. 7-16	7-12
They also made inquiries as to prices in different parts of the same states, and this is their finding and report in that regard:
At Minot, North Dakota, close to the Canadian border and almost immediately south of Regina, the price of ordinary gas is 21-5 cents a gallon. In Regina the price is 32-5 cents, 11 cents a gallon more than the Minot price. At Scobey, Montana, just over the border from Saskatchewan, gasoline costs only 28-8 cents.

Price of Gasoline-Mr. Bennett
These American prices are adjusted to the imperial gallon.
In Montana cities there is uniformity in gasoline prices. In North Dakota the same situation is apparent.
On the Canadian prairies there are all sorts of prices. There is two cents difference between the Saskatoon and Regina prices, and in Winnipeg gasoline is selling at 7J cents less than in Regina.
There are big oil refineries in Calgary, Regina, and Winnipeg, but there are not two cities in western Canada with similar figures for gasoline.
We understand at this time that the matter of gasoline prices is being brought before the Saskatchewan legislature, possibly before all the prairie legislatures. They are or intend investigating the matter from a somewhat different angle. We believe here-and this is a matter over which the house has control- that the difference in price is largely attributable to the exploiting that the oil companies are doing by reason of the tariff legislation of 1930. We believe that although some 80 per cent of our gasoline is produced in Canada and only 20 per cent imported, the producers in this country are holding their prices right up to what gasoline could be obtained at from the other side, even with the fixed valuations, the dumping duty being added on those fixed valuations, and the regular duty. We believe the oil companies are taking advantage of everything the tariff allows them, and there has not been a decrease in gasoline prices to the same extent that there has been in prices of other goods. For these reasons we are asking that this matter be referred to a committee in order that there may be a thorough investigation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with
great interest to the observations of the hon. members for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) and Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell). It is always well, however, not to prejudge a case on its presentation. I shall therefore refrain from endeavouring to traverse in any respect the allegations that have been made. There is one thing I think I should fairly say, and that is that it is not correct to assume that because we produce gasoline in this country, the raw material from which it is produced is produced in Canada. Unfortunately, except for small quantities of crude naphtha found in Turner valley and very small quantities of crude petroleum found in other places, we are entirely dependent, for the production of gasoline in Canada, on imported raw material.

The crude petroleum is brought in not only from Columbia and Peru, but from other parts of the world as well.
The agitation in connection with an investigation into the prices of gasoline has been going on for some time in this country. The observations made by the hon. member for Swift Current first started the discussion last year, and it has been continued with more or less vigour ever since. It will be recalled that the great producing oil companies gave an undertaking at the time that the tariffs were changed in 1930, and by that undertaking they are bound. That, coupled with the provisions of the statute, sufficiently indicates the position of the administration. But owing to the discussions that have taken place in the public press, on public platforms and elsewhere, apparently the companies themselves have been seized of these agitations and discussions, and on the 19th of January the Imperial Oil Limited wrote to me a letter reading as follows:
Rt. Hon. R. B. Bennett, P.C.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir.-
Due to chaotic conditions in the United States, the widespread evasion of gasoline taxes there and to uninformed criticism of the petroleum industry in Canada, an impression has been created that undue profits are being exacted by the industry from the Canadian public. We believe it to be in our own interest, as -well as that of the government, that the situation, in respect to gasoline prices, should be thoroughly ventilated.
Our willingness to submit ourselves to inquiry by any competent tribunal is largely prompted by the beneficial results to us which followed the last public investigation, which was conducted at the instance of the government of Ontario, but which was not limited in scope to the jurisdiction of that province.
Voluntarily, all of the refining companies with head offices in Ontario submitted every detail of their business, Canadian and foreign, to the government. The investigation, which covered a period of five years, occupied months; every document required was produced and executives of all the companies concerned were examined under oath.
The finding was that in the years 1920 to 1924 inclusive, the earnings of these Canadian companies had averaged 8 per cent, and that in no year were they exorbitant. The effect of this upon public opinion was extremely helpful.
Actually, the Canadian consumer is now enjoying lower prices for gasoline and other petroleum products than at any time during the period covered by the investigation referred to and the industry is now working upon a narrower spread over raw material costs than then.

Price of Gasoline-Mr. Carmichael
As a matter of self interest and because the true position cannot be brought before the public in any other way, except at great expense, we wish to advise your government that any inquiry which it may decide to conduct will be facilitated by us.
Yours respectfully,
Victor Ross,
Vice-President, Imperial Oil, Limited.
The fallowing communication, dated January 16, 1932, was received from the McColl-Frontenac Oil Company Limited:
Dear Sir,-
During the last few months there have appeared from time to time, either as speeches in the Canadian House of Commons or as articles in the press, charges that the Canadian [DOT]oil companies have been treating the public unfairly regarding gasoline prices. More recently there have appeared requests from various sources for an investigation by a royal commission appointed by the Canadian House of Commons.
Should such a commission be appointed, I would like to assure you that our company will assist in every way the workings of such commission and be pleased to place before the members all facts pertaining to the operations of our company.
Yours very truly,
McColl-Frontenac Oil Company Limited, J. A. Wales,
Vice-President.
The following letter, dated February 6, 1932, *was received from the British American Oil Company Limited:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister,-
I note in Votes and Proceedings of the House of Commons of Canada, dated February 4th, notice of motion by Mr. Thos. F. Donnelly, member for Willow Bunch, Saskatchewan, dealing with the price of gasoline to the Canadian consumer.
There has been considerable comment, particularly in western Canada, concerning the price of gasoline compared with the price in the United States, and an investigation would clarify the situation, both from the standpoint of the oil companies and the public. Therefore, on behalf of this company, I advise that I shall be pleased to offer the fullest cooperation should an investigation be determined upon.
I would point out, however, that the manufacture and national distribution of gasoline involves a very comprehensive system of accounting and, therefore, the commission appointed should be technically competent to deal with the situation.
Yoprs very truly,
A. L. Ellsworth,
President.
I shall therefore make no further comment upon the motion other than to indicate that so far as the government is concerned the motion will be adopted in the terms in which it has been prepared. I might say that it is 41761-9
just possible that a smaller committee would be of greater service for those who are putting forward the views that they express, but in order that there may be no misapprehension or misunderstanding or misconception the government will accept the motion in the exact terms in which it was submitted to this house, and in which it was submitted to the press before it was discussed here.
In view of the representations that have been made by the three largest companies vitally affected, I shall not, as I say, discuss the merits or demerits of the observations that have been made with respect to this matter. To prejudge is not the duty of government, but the fullest possible opportunity so far as the facilities of the committee are concerned will be afforded for the investigation, and in the light of the willingness expressed by the three largest manufacturers of gasoline from petroleum in this country I should think there would be no reason why definite results should not follow from the labours of the committee. The committee may require some technical assistance, and that technical assistance will not be denied.

I was pleased indeed to hear the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) acceding to the request of the -mover of the motion (Mr. Donnelly) to have a committee investigate the price of gasoline. If this matter is to go before the banking and commerce committee, of which I have not previously been a member, I feel like making a few comments which might be helpful to the committee.
I represent a constituency that is, I might say, altogether agricultural. We have large farms of open prairie country which are operated largely by means of the tractor. We have also the combine in use out there, and the motor car, of course, so that gasoline is used very extensively in my constituency. There has been a feeling for some time among the farmers of my district that the price of gasoline is too high. I do not know whether that feeling is warranted or not, and I welcome the opportunity to have the matter properly investigated in a committee so that the correct information may be brought out. In my own district the retail price of gasoline in the -past year has been 35 cents per gallon. That includes 5 cents per gallon for provincial tax, leaving the retail price to the motorist 30 cents per gallon. If the gasoline is for tractor purposes there is a slight reduction in the price because of the larger quantity taken. I have here a letter from the secretary of a



Price of Gasoline-Mr. Carmichael
municipality in my constituency, which perhaps is worthy of presentation to the house. He says:
I am instructed to write you in protest of the duty of 2J cents on gasoline from the United States as a result of which the Canadian consumer has been paying from three to five cents more for gasoline than his competitor in the United States.
I do not know whether that statement is correct or not. He says further:
At a time when agriculture is in such a desperate condition that a very large number of farmers are faced with "downing tools" it is absolutely impossible to carry on under present economic conditions, we feel that you, representing a western agricultural constituency, must see the injustice of increasing costs to the power farmer at a time when it is imperative that everything possible should be done to reduce these to the minimum in order to allow him to continue to exist.
That represents to a large extent the feeling at least among the power farmers in my own constituency.
There are several factors that enter into the price of gasoline, and I shall briefly mention them. One is referred to in this letter-the tariff. Prior to September, 1930, the general tariff on gasoline was one cent per gallon, with some grades coming in free. In September, 1930, the duty was raised to 2^ cents per gallon, and we were assured by the leader of the house that any attempt to increase the price of gasoline because of the increased duty would be speedily dealt with. So we have an effective weapon to deal with this matter if it should 'be proven in the committee that advantage has been taken of the tariff. Another important factor bearing on the price of gasoline is the power that rests in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue to set an arbitrary value for duty purposes on gasoline coming in from the United States. Last year there was a price war on in some of the western states and out our way the people were of the opinion that gasoline was down to a very low price in Oklahoma; yet when that gasoline came to the border the Canadian purchaser was compelled to pay duty on a value arbitrarily set by the Minister of National Revenue. That is a feature that could be inquired into by the committee.
Another factor that enters into the price of gasoline is the freight rate. I have a letter here from another municipal council protesting against the high freight rate on gasoline and asking that as a measure of relief for agriculture the freight rate should be cut in half. I do not know whether that is a feasible proposition or not.

Another fact that is perhaps unknown to a great many of the membere here is that gasoline does not weigh up per gallon to the weight 'used in charging freight. I quote from a letter from the secretary of a municipal council in my constituency. He says:
We find upon examination of freight bills of tank ears of gasoline coming to this point that they are billed with the weight figured on the basis of eight pounds to the gallon, and when a gallon is weighed out it turns the scale at seven pounds.
The average car will run over 6,000 gallons so that the consumer pays freight as a rule on three tons of gasoline which is not carried by the company and never received by the dealer which turns out roughly at $50 per car.
If that is correct, it seems to me that the committee might take notice of it, and have the difficulty rectified. This secretary protests also against the high price of gasoline, and asks for a reduction in the freight rate charges as a relief to agriculture.
There is another feature to which I should like to direct the attention of hon. members. During the past season in my own district a number of farmers and residents have gone across the border into the province of Alberta, a matter of about fifty miles, and purchased what they called distillate at 15 cents a gallon, with no tax payable to either the province of Alberta or the province of Saskatchewan. I am informed that distillate is superior to gasoline for motor car purposes, if you are content to bear with the odour arising from it. So far as power is concerned it seems to test a little higher than refined gasoline. In any case a great many of the residents of my own constituency have been crossing the border into the province of Alberta, purchasing this cheaper product and using it both in their tractors and in motor cars. I understand the distillate is secured in the Turner Valley field of Alberta, and I suggest that if it serves the purpose and can be purchased at a price so much lower than that of distilled gasoline, it is worthy of investigation.
There are several questions now in the public mind which should be answered. From my own constituency I received the following:
In order to obtain a Canadian refining industry employing 4,978 persons with a pay-roll of $8,153,625 we are subsidizing the owners of the refineries to the extent of some $20,000,000.
I do not know whether' or not that is a correct statement, but .possibly the committee would investigate as to whether or not the owners of the refineries are being subsidized to that extent. If I understood the Prime Minister correctly, I believe his statement was that their dividends were about 8 per cent. To

Price oj Gasoline-Mr. Brown
my mind that is a very handsome dividend in these times of depression, and if they are receiving that amount they are very well cared for indeed.
I am very happy to give my endorsation to this resolution. I should like to see a thorough investigation made, and all interested parties brought before the committee. I am not sure that the committee on banking and commerce is the best place to investigate this matter, and it might have been well had the mover recommended a special committee to delve into the problem and make a more thorough and impartial investigation than the committee on banking and commerce could make. I am content, however, to endorse the proposed investigation, and I hope that something useful may come from it.

I had intended to make a few remarks along the line followed by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). To my mind the order of reference should be sufficiently large to allow the committee to investigate the prices of kerosene and fuel oil.
And of petroleum products.

Yes, and of petroleum products. When I arrived home last summer I found that the oil companies were charging a price for kerosene that the farmers felt was unwarranted, and as a result they began to import the distillate to which the hon. member has referred. I think however he is mistaken when he refers to distillate as a substitute for gasoline, because as a matter of fact it is a substitute for kerosene to be used in tractor engines. The farmers in my constituency were importing distillate from the United States, paying a duty thereon and finding the importation profitable as compared with the price they were paying for kerosene. The oil companies then reduced the price of kerosene, and I believe there was an undertaking that the reduced price would continue during the summer. The reduction in price indicated that they were evidently very anxious to sell their product. Then, some time during the month of December, notice was given that the price of kerosene would be raised 3 cents per gallon.
To my mind the committee would do well to inquire as to whether there was anything in the general conditions of trade which warranted the increase of 3 cents per gallon in the month of December, or whether the oil 41761-9J
companies took advantage of an opportunity to charge a higher price to the householders who were buying kerosene for lighting purposes and, to a somewhat limited degree, for use in engines. I think therefore that the order of reference should be sufficiently large to include not only gasoline but all petroleum products.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I heard with much pleasure the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) before six o'clock to the effect that he was going to offer no objection to this resolution. It was gratifying also to hear the definite terms in which he stated that the fullest investigation would be permitted; and his offer to furnish such technical assistance as might be required. The right hon. gentleman read us certain letters from some of the Canadian oil companies, indicating their willingness to cooperate in any such investigation; that is satisfactory also.
During the dinner recess I had time to consider and in some sort perhaps to analyse those letters and seek to find in them what the line of presentation of the companies would be when the matter comes before the special committee. I find references to a very comprehensive system of bookkeeping and a quite proper suggestion that technicians would need to be available to understand that complicated system. There were also references to a previous investigation which had taken place under the auspices of the government of Ontario, which investigation, it was stated, had occupied many months and had demonstrated that over a period of some four years no profits in excess of 8 per cent had been derived by the Canadian companies in question. I think the deduction is a fair one- I do not wish to be anything but that-that their attitude would be that if they could prove that the Canadian companies had not taken undue profits in recent months or years, they might be allowed to continue the range of gasoline prices as at present existing in Canada.
Now*, sir, I submit that that is emphatically not the issue, and that justice will not be done nor the public satisfied if the line of investigation is confined entirely to that point,
Price of Gasoline-Mr. Neill

although, of course, the investigation would include it. I maintain the issue is rather this: have the companies taken advantage of the increase of tariff and of the special provisions and amendments made to the Customs Act in September, 1930, to maintain the prices of gasoline in Canada at a level higher than the comparable level of prices in any competing country-in this case the United States? That is the question which is being asked at the street corners, at business men's luncheons, at farmers' conventions and at fishermens' meetings. The speeches to-day on the resolution all bore out that trend of thought. If the answer is, yes, that they have been taking advantage of this legislation, then, of course, it is obvious that the government should take the action that they indicated in September, 1930.
I see nothing in the correspondence pointing to any intention to answer the point that I have just made, that is, the relative prices of gasoline in Canada and in other competing countries. It will not suffice for the Canadian companies merely to prove on paper that they have taken no excess profits in the recent period. To combat that would necessitate our going very far back and investigating records-not open to us-of the oil companies dominant in the United States. We would have to go into the question of interlocking interests, of a division of assets in years perhaps long gone by, whether the relationship of parent and child did not or does not exist between some of the oil companies in a foreign country and in Canada, and whether the parent on some occasions did not get the best of the deal. I am only suggesting the point. Possibly there might be a common source of supply to the parent and the child, and possibly better prices might have been given to the one rather than to the other. That is something which it would be impossible for us to prove by any information that we could obtain. There would also enter into the matter the question of watered stock, the question of bonuses of stock, of stock issued as dividends, and whether stock so issued should be entitled to claim interest.
As the member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) stated this afternoon, he had personal knowledge of where he could buy gas cheaper retail in the states than he could buy it wholesale in Canada; possibly some of our Canadian profits have been going to meet the close competition in the states. Many of these things it is absolutely impossible to ascertain, or to say whether under the circumstances 8 per

cent or one per cent is a fair dividend, whether 8 per cent represents really 8 per cent or a very much larger figure. I recall when I went into business many years ago naturally I met with competition, and it was my endeavour to keep prices so low as to eliminate that competition. But occasionally some big company would get the opportunity to buy a whole carload of some commodity and sell it at cost, or perhaps below cost-what they would call a "special," which probably they figured was a cheap form of advertising. But when my customers came to me complaining of my higher price it was useless for me to show my invoices as proofs that I was paying more for the article than the price at which the big company was selling it. Nor was it any use for me to suggest that the company had paid more for the article than the price at which they were retailing it. My customers were not interested in that at all; the only thing they were concerned about was, could they get the article somewhere else at a price cheaper than that at which they could get it from me. I very soon realized that it was a waste of time to argue that I must have a particular price to give me a fair profit. They were not interested in my welfare, and it was up to me to meet my competitor's price or lose a certain amount of business. The converse was true when a fortunate turn in the market enabled me to buy to advantage and I could sell below my competitors; the public did not ask me whether I was making much or little profit on my sales.
The point I am trying to make is this; there is no obligation whatever on us to maintain prices to give a profit to any oil company any more than there was any obligation on the public to give me profits on my petty line of business. It might just as well be argued that we should provide dividends by way of increased freight rates to the Canadian railways. Of course, if some members of the house held Canadian Pacific Railway shares it would be very gratifying to them if we could arrange for an 8 per cent return on their investment; but I see no disposition in this house or in the country to do that. What about our friend's from the prairies if they come forward and show beyond peradventure that they cannot grow wheat profitably at a price below $1 a bushel, are we to formulate policies or vote money to enable them to get that price? We are just as much entitled to do that as to provide any given rate of dividend for an oil company. It is not our business, especially in

Price oj Gasoline-Mr. Neill
these days when profits are so minimized, to provide guaranteed profits to anybody.
This is the question:	Are they meeting
competitive prices without sheltering or-profit-eering under the terms of the tariff? If not, it is the duty of the committee to so report and of the government to take appropriate action.
As the government have consented to the passing of the resolution, I will not waste time supporting it in regard to the gas used in cars and tractors, which has been the subject of debate this afternoon; but I do want to say a very few words in connection with another branch of the question which has not been touched upon to-day, and that is as to how the price of gasoline affects the fishing industry-more particularly the small fisherman, because the big fishing companies use expensive Diesel engines and a cheaper fuel in their large boats which the small fisherman cannot afford to buy. It may be said that the automobile is an important or a trivial adjunct of the man in business; but as regards the fisherman, it is absolutely essential that his boat should be fitted with a gasoline engine. When dealers sell us cars they tell us they will go 25 or 30 miles on a gallon of gasoline, but it is a known fact that the average fishing boat cannot go more than 5, 6 or 7 miles on a gallon.
This afternoon the right hon. Prime Minister very kindly gave credit to ' the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) and the hon. member for Willow Bunch for introducing this matter last session, but so far as the needs of the fishermen are concerned I think I can claim for the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) and myself credit for the fact that we antedated those gentlemen in bringing up this question. When the legislation was introduced in September of 1939 the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth and myself pleaded with the government to have mercy on the fishermen, explaining their dire need and their inability to meet increased taxation. We went so far as to move an amendment which was rejected, and why was it rejected? A reference was made to the guarantees which had been given by the oil companies, and at page 533 the right hon. gentleman said very definitely:
I am quite sure that both hon. gentlemen realize that as there is to be no increase in price there is no object in what they suggest. . .
That was with reference to the amendment. At page 597 the right hon. gentleman also said:
There will be no increase in price.
That was one of the reasons why the amendment was rejected. Again, the question arose as to the guarantees given by the oil companies. It was stated that they only referred to there being no increase in price, and this question was raised: Suppose as a matter of fact, while there is no increase, there is no drop in price when there should be? At page 578, in two places, the right hon. Prime Minister dealt very frankly and fully with that suggestion. On the second occasion he said quite plainly:
... if there should be a great falling-off pf prices beside us and an effort made to maintain present prices in Canada, that would be utilizing the tariff to increase the prices and would be a violation of the undertaking.
So whether the price of gasoline was increased or whether it was not reduced when that should have been done, the obligation of the companies would be the same.
The results have been outlined this afternoon by all the hon. members who have spoken, and they have repeatedly shown very plainly the great difference in prices between those in the United States and those in corresponding points in Canada. No mention was made of the great spread in prices between points in the extreme west, such as Seattle and Vancouver. The difference there is greater than at other points named this afternoon. I should like to give just one illustration from a fishing point of view; I should like to get it on Hansard. The increase in duty from one cent to 2i cents a gallon was not the chief trouble, though that was equivalent to an increase of 250 per cent in the duty. Still, the country voted for high protection in 1930, and cannot very well complain if it gets high protection, and the 2i cents would appear to be high enough. But that could be endured, perhaps; that has not caused the trouble. The difficulty has been brought about by those changes in the Customs Act, more particularly under section 36. There have been several separate changes, which have made it possible to enormously enhance the duty by means of orders in council.
There are several methods by which this may be done. One is by putting on a price which the customs department considers to be the fair price or cost price in the competing country, plus a fair charge for distribution costs, plus a fair profit. Another method is the more arbitrary one of simply passing an order in council in which the minister declares the value to be whatever he wishes.
I said I wished to give an illustration. This is an actual case, in connection with which I

Price of Gasoline-Mr. Neill
think I could produce proofs if necessary. It has to do with fishermen going to Seattle with fish caught in the waters off Vancouver island. These were taken to the only market available at that - time, which was Seattle. In order to make the comparison fair I will translate the prices into .terms of imperial gallons. They could buy gasoline in Seattle for 7.2 cents per imperial gallon but, while that was the price at which it was being sold by millions of gallons all down the Pacific coast, our Department of National Revenue ruled that this was not the proper price. They would not allow the people of the United States to fix the -price at which they could sell their gasoline; they decided that the correct price should be 13.2 cents, a difference of 6 cents, and of course under -the provisions of the Customs Act there automatically came into force a so-called dumping duty of 6 cents per gallon. In addition there was the regular duty of 2J cents, making a total duty of 8.5 -cents on ga-soline which cost only 7.2 cents! But even if you add those figures together they fall far short of what was then the current price in British Columbia. The United States fisherman was competing with our fisherman on the same fishing grounds, paying only 7.2 cents -for his gasoline, paying less for his engine, but getting 2 cents more per pound for his fish because of -the duty of 2 cents per pound on our fish going into the United States.
, I sa'd in June last this creates, perhaps inadvertently, a very great hardship on our fishing population. We talk about Canada first and about equal opportunity, but this situation does n-ot reveal an equal opportunity for our west coast fishermen, though it might be called perhaps a little better than an equ-al opportunity for the oil -companies.
To know that the fishermen are in desperate need one has only to -be familiar with current conditions in the fishing industry on the west coast. Not only have prices been shot to an unbelievable extent, but in -many cases the market has totally disappeared. Last year the prices went so low that good salmon was bringing one cent a pound, and it is claimed by those in -a position to know that the cost of gasoline is 35 per cent of the cost of fishing, so it will be seen that when our fishermen have to pay 22 cents -per gallon for gasoline it gives a tremendous advantage to those with whom they have to compete. I should -like to quote just a few wards from a press item to illustrate this fact:
The run of sockeye is so far very poor. High boat got 15 fish at 6 cents per pound which will average around 20 cents per fish.

In other -words the high -boat, fishing perhaps 18 or 20 hours a day, made about $3, while the low boat would make probably around SI. I quote again:
Many trollers have quit and gone ashore. Fish are costing the fishermen more to catch than they get for them from the dealers. Gas here is 22 cents per gallon while it is sold to fishermen across the line at 8 cents. It costs on an average one gallon per hour to keep the trailer moving, some more, some less, but boats do not on an average catch more than one fish per hour at 15 cents per fish.
Then -the article goes on to give the price of one cent per pound, which I mentioned a moment ago.
That is the situation I wish to bring to the attention of the house -in order that it may be on record when this question is referred to the banking a-nd commerce -committee, of which I am not a member. I want it to be there so that this phase of the question will not ibe -misunderstood, but I repeat -that I am pleased with the attitude of the government in the matter and I hope the work of the committee will be of benefit -to users of gasoline -both on sea and on land.

Is the house ready for the question?
-Mr. BROWN: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question. He was not in the house when I spoke on this matter just before six o'clock. I suggested the desirability of enlarging the order of reference so os to include -all petroleum products. Would he care to accept that suggestion?
There has been no move on the -part of the mover and the seconder of the resolution to adopt -that suggestion.
Motion agreed to.

PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
Whereas during the session of 1931 a special committee -was appointed to investigate the "Beauharnois power development" and
Whereas it was shown that enormous sums of money had been contributed for political campaign funds,
Be it resolved: That, in the opinion of this house, it is desirable that the committee on privileges and elections consider and report upon the question of election funds and draft such amendments to the elections act as may be considered necessary.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it was not -my intention to speak so early in the deliberations

Elections Act-Mr. Mitchell
of this house, 'because the experience I have gained from other deliberative bodies is that it is desirable first to gain some background and understand more fully the rules and procedure which govern. During the recent campaign in which I was successful one of the outstanding issues was the Beauharnois scandal and its relationship to campaign funds. The evidence in that regard is definite. I quote from the Toronto Globe of August 18, 1931, as follows:
Mr. Sweezey's evidence summed up the campaign contributions as follows:
Dominion Liberals	 $720,000
Ontario Conservative party.. ..	125,000
Quebec Conservative party..	. .	30,000
Ontario Liberal party	 2,000
or 3,000
Mr. Leslie Bell, Montreal Conservative member	 6,000
From this I think we can all readily agree that the Child rests upon the doorstep of both the Conservative and Liberal parties.
The resolution which I have the honour to move is definite in its terms. It reflects the driving force of public opinion, not only in the province of Ontario and particularly in the constituency which I represent, but throughout the whole Dominion. It should be remembered that apart from the hon. member who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Bourgeois) I come most directly from the people of this country, and I carry a message which interprets their desire that this problem of campaign funds must be confronted and that an honest effort must be made to prevent its recurrence in the political life of this country. I am glad to say that as a representative of Labour I received the support not only of the working people but also of the middle classes and the more well-to-do. These people were amazed at the magnitude of this scandal, which, after all is said and done, strikes at the very roots of democratic government. Many men spent last Christmas within the confines of Kingston penitentiary who had done less than these gentlemen have done, many of whom no doubt spent the holiday season surrounded by the comforts of a first class hotel.
I submit that we have come to a sorry pass when these financial highwaymen can influence indirectly the votes of the people of this country. Money is still an influence in the elections of Canada. Some time ago a well known politician was discussing an election campaign with me. Like all other candidates I expressed the belief that I was going to win, but he replied, "Humphrey, we have the dough and you have the enthusiasm, but we
will win." What chance have men with progressive views to win an election when they are pitted against conditions such as this? It is my experience that men with progressive views are generally poor, and being poor economically and socially, they have a terrible struggle to maintain their existence.
I remember well the campaigns which brought into existence in the province of Ontario what I consider to be the greatest public ownership project upon the face of this globe. Up until recently any Canadian, irrespective of the province from which he came, could go to any part of this world and speak with pride of that public ownership proposition. Electricity is one of the greatest civilizing forces in the life of this country; but what chance has this project when it is confronted by something similar to this Beauharnois business? All hon. members who are farmers by profession, whether Conservative or Liberal in politics, must realize that electrical power is the greatest Jersey cow in existence-it is easy to milk.
I know something of the problems which confront a Labour candidate during an election. In many cases he is forced to go on earning his livelihood; money is not coming in very fast and all the problems which confront the average candidate are intensified. If this condition is allowed to continue, what chance have the democratic institutions of this country? Frankly, I believe the Dominion could give a lead to the world on the question of the conduct of elections so far as the financial aspect is concerned. I believe we could pioneer in this regard and show the world that elections can be won on principle and not on the driving force of selfish financial corporations.
Briefly, what are the facts? We all agree that campaign funds are necessary; we all agree that they are desirable, and I think that on a consideration of the evidence we all agree that some of them have been contributed by people who have axes to grind. Let me ask the house: is this a satisfactory way of influencing public opinion? In connection with that, I should like to read an account of an incident which took place, I understand, in the last provincial election in Quebec, where one of the candidates accused another of taking $325,000 from the Beauharnois corporation. This is the reply of that particular candidate:
I hereby state with all the force at my command that never directly or indirectly did I receive a cent from that organization.
He went so far as to charge the candidate who made the accusation as "a vulgar liar
136	COMMONS
Elections Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
and a public calumniator." These were not two highwaymen talking to one another. One was Mr. Gagnon and the other was Mr. Taschereau. Another instance that is worth while quoting I take from the Toronto Globe of Tuesday, August 18, 1931. It reads:
Nor can the general question of campaign funds be kept in the background. At the meeting where Mr. Taschereau flung his challenge to Mr. Gagnon, Mr. Laetere Roy, former member for Levis, discussing the political contribution of the Beauharnois company made this statement:
"During the last federal election the Conservatives had $2,500,000 at their disposal. You know yourselves that in Levis they had barrels of money. And do you know where that money came from? A good part from a railway corporation, and the larger amount from the manufacturers. Mr. Bennett then raised the tariff which allowed them some return for the sums they had advanced."
I am an Englishman, and I am proud of the fact. Of course we are not responsible for our nationality; we had no control over that. Possibly if some of us had, we would not be here now. My attitude in life towards the human family anyway is that we are all human beings. I want, however, to bring up this point:	the only argument I know of
in favour of titles is that you can get some rich people to pay for titles half a million dollars which go into the campaign fund of a political party, but in this democratic country of ours, they are repaid not in titles but in cold cash.
In conclusion, I appreciate the complexity of the problem that will confront the committee, but I believe, after what has arisen out of that investigation, the house owes a duty to the people of this Dominion to see to it that as far as is humanly possible there shall be no recurrence of the present scandal in the public life of this country. Even if this should mean a distinct and possibly radical departure in connection with the operation of elections, it is the duty of the house to see to it that that departure is made forthwith.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
relieved of the preamble, the resolution reads:
Be it resolved: that, in the opinion of this house, it is desirable that the committee on privileges and elections consider and report upon the question of election funds and draft such amendments to the election act as may be considered necessary.
I am heartily in favour of that motion carrying, and I hope it will meet with the unanimous acceptance of the house. Indeed, the resolution is almost in the exact terms of what at the conclusion of the last session of

parliament I suggested should be the first step taken at the beginning of the present session, namely that a select committee of the house should be appointed to consider the question of election funds and amendments to the election act which would be in the public interest. The present resolution suggests the standing committee on privileges and elections. I do not think there is much to choose between the two. The committee on privileges and elections is a proper committee to dea^ with a matter of this kind. The main point is that there should be at this session a careful consideration of the whole question of campaign funds so called, and if possible, amendments to the election act which, as I said, will be in the public interest.
When I spoke in this house on July 30 last, I went a step further and suggested that it was desirable to have a royal commission to inquire into the whole question of campaign funds, not only of the last campaign, but as well of the campaigns of 1925 and 1926. I repeated that proposal at a meeting which I addressed at London, Ontario, on October 20, my view being that were a royal commission appointed at that time the personnel of which would include commissioners nominated at the instance of the three principal parties in the house-because that is the only kind of royal commission that would meet with any degree of public confidence in a matter of this kind-we would have before us at the beginning of this session a report which would be a great help to the house, or to a committee of this sort in deciding upon necessary amendments to the act. The government, however, alone has power to appoint a royal commission, and the government has not seen its way or thought it wise to take that step. It must of course accept the responsibility therefor.
I should like to quote from Hansard of July 30 of last year what I said with reference to these two matters I shall quote just sufficient to make clear that I am but restating at the moment the position I then took. I said, as will appear at pages 438S-9 of Hansard of July 30 last:
I think that not only should there be a royal commission to go into the matter of party campaign funds from the ground up, so that if at all possible we may have the matter cleared up once and for all, but as soon as the next session of parliament meets there should be appointed a select committee of the house to consider the Dominion Elections Act, and see if in some way it is not possible to have that act further amended so as to render unnecessary, to as large a degree as possible, the collection of moneys for campaign purposes. I make that

Elections Act-Mr. Bennett
suggestion in the interests of every hon. member in the house, in the interest of every future candidate, in the interests of every political party, and in the public interest.
Hon. members will see that the course there suggested is practically identical with the one which the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) has recommended in the motion which is before the house and which I have expressed the hope the house will adopt unanimously. I did at the time make, in addition, certain suggestions as to what might be helpful by way of amendments to the elections act to accomplish the purpose in view.
I shall not repeat those suggestions at the moment. No doubt if a committee is appointed they will come before the committee, and if they do, I hope that they will be favourably considered.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
May I congratulate the hon. member
for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) on his maiden speech in this chamber? It is quite clear that he is a skilled public speaker and a debater of large experience. His performance was most creditable and I trust will be often repeated in this chamber, as often as may be necessary to meet the circumstances that seem in his judgment to require his intervening in debate.
There is only one question to be considered in connection with the motion now before us, and that is whether or not any good purpose will be served by dealing with the matter at this session. When the census returns are complete it will be necessary to readjust the boundaries of the constituencies, and a complete redistribution will pass this house. It is obvious that the census returns will not be completed to enable that to be done at this session. In point of fact they never have been. Next session will therefore be the first opportunity at which redistribution can be considered.
Side by side with redistribution the whole machinery of elections must be considered. For instance, the question as to whether or not our method of registering the voters is a sound one; secondly, whether or not there should be any educational test imposed. I recall on one occasion having endeavoured to have the registers set up by each elector subscribing his name in a book, and then when he came to vote, if his identity were challenged, he would of course have to sign, and it would become apparent then, if he were a repeater, that he was not the elector entitled to vote. I need hardly say that repeating has in this country assumed very considerable proportions. I recall on one occasion being
told at the end of a contested election in a city through which I was passing that a certain visitor from another city, a foreign city, had voted some forty times that day and had left on the evening train. That is one difficulty that has to be overcome. In Great Britain they can have a general election after a very short interval. Here the shortest time within which an election can now be held is some fifty-six days. That is a matter that should engage the attention of those charged with responsibility for the enactment of a new elections act. The other day, for instance, a vacancy occurred in Athabasca. It was quite apparent from the communications that were sent that unless that election were held while the ground was still frozen it might be impossible to hold it at all until well on in the summer, and indeed it might be difficult to hold it at all within the time required by law. You will find that that happens frequently in this country. How can that difficulty be overcome?
Then you have the larger question, to which some attention has been directed, as to corruption in elections. The hon. member for East Hamilton said that there had been evidence of corrupt elections in this country. There have been. Elections have been held in this country in which a very large number of those returned have been charged with participating in fraudulent arrangements whereby they were elected, and the legislature has passed a statute to prevent the matter being inquired into by the courts. That is a matter, of course, that is well understood. Each legislature and parliament chooses its own methods of dealing with these matters. In England and in Canada, both in the federal parliament and in the provincial legislatures, it was the custom, as is well known, in the beginning of the development of our institutions for committees of the house to determine whether or not a member had been properly elected, and it will be within the memory of those who took the trouble to read the history of it that when Wilkes was elected over Colonel Luttrell, although he had a clear majority, the House of Commons undertook to change the return and substitute for the name of Wilkes that of Colonel Luttrell. It will perhaps be within the memory of members of this house that that brought about well nigh a revolution; for it was said that the legislature was not the body charged with responsibility for the election of members, but rather the people of the country, who had already exercised their franchise and returned Mr. Wilkes. That doctrine no longer avails in some parts of this country, and a

Elections Act-Mr. Bennett
legislature has seen fit to determine that it, and not the electors, shall say who shall sit in the legislature. I direct attention to that only as indicating the trend of modern democratic thought. In the early days in England, in the middle of the last century, it was believed, as it has been in this country, that the proper method of determining these matters was through the courts; and hence it is that judges-in our country two judges- are called upon to decide whether or not a member has been legally elected to his seat if a petition has been filed against his return.
The causes that vacate a seat are so numerous, Mr. Speaker, that it is almost impossible to say with certainty that any election held in this country might not on purely technical grounds be voided. I point that out to the hon. member for East Hamilton; for we are dealing with practical things, and not with matters of the emotions. When he says that it is desirable to do thus and so I only point out that in the election law that has been on the statute books of this country since we substituted the courts for a committee of parliament we have made so many matters offences under the act that almost any election could be voided. In the end the machinery of the law has very seldom been used. Those are facts known to everyone in this country. Such things, for instance, as the employment of automobiles, the giving of a dinner or a lunch to a friend under certain circumstances, the giving of hospitality of any kind-

speechtext:
Not necessarily a drink.
Hospitality and ginger ale, for instance. It is true that there are constituents of hon. gentlemen present who probably prefer a mixture of alcohol with water to ginger ale, but that need not engage our attention. The point I desire to make is this. For nearly three-quarters of a century we have had upon the statute books in Canada, in Great Britain, in Australia and other countries under the British flag, provisions whereby elections could be voided for corrupt acts; we have endeavoured to define them, and in so doing we have made the conduct of an ordinary election almost technically illegal under the provisions of the statute. Shall that continue as it is? That is something to be considered. Is it wise thus to impose restrictions against what I might call the common sense attitude of most men in these matters? If you meet your friend, take him in to dinner and extend to him hospitality of that kind, are you laying

yourself open to a possible offence and to the voiding of an election? This question which arises out of kindred circumstances need not be discussed beyond saying that I have always held the view that if we would limit the number of offences and make them broad and general without endeavouring to particularize as we have done, we would find it less difficult to attain the end we have in mind with respect to the voiding of elections.
You will remember perhaps, sir, that the late Doctor Weldon, who at the time was dean of the law school at Halifax, to whom I owe a debt I will never be able to repay, and whose memory I revere, sought by motion made in .this house to disfranchise constituencies for corrupt acts that resulted in the return of a member who should not have been returned. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I have long held the view that there is much to be said in support of that principle. If the constituency is willing to be debauched by a candidate violating the provisions of the statute and committing such corrupt acts as are defined by the law, resulting in the voiding of the election, it might be that if it were proven to be general the constituency itself could be punished for a term of two or three years, or as the case might merit.

speechtext: But, sir, we have gone a step farther. We have undertaken to punish the constituencies and to punish those guilty of corrupt offences, and we have defined what constitutes corrupt acts. Will anybody say we have made substantial progress in twenty-five or thirty years in that regard? Read election reports in cases where elections were contested-you will find them in the library- and I think you will express great surprise that a seat could be voided under circumstances there stated. In one of the first cases-in fact, I think it is the first case reported in the Supreme court reports-there was reference to undue influence in connection with those who exercised their franchise. All these things are now past and gone, and no one will say, contrasting present day conditions with the allegations made in the case to which I have referred, that we have made very great progress in that regard. Why? The hon. member for East. Hamilton was very frank when he said that campaign funds are necessary. I recall reading, during the progress of his campaign, a letter in which the president of the Trades and Labour Council enclosed a subscription to assist the hon. gentleman who is now the member for East Hamilton in his election campaign. Undoubtedly that subscription was to help defray legitimate costs in connection with the campaign. There are legitimate costs; there are legitimate expenses, and the fact that your friend or my friend-

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
If I said Trades and
Labour Council I meant to say Trades and Labour Congress. I was not responsible for the donation being made public, and I have merely mentioned that I read in the newspaper that Mr. Moore had sent a contribution to the hon. gentleman. I did not complain of his action, and I am not criticizing it. I merely point out that the hon. gentleman has
stated frankly in this chamber that campaign funds are essential and necessary to play their part in an election. Whether the cheque was personal or how it came to be paid I cannot say, but I do know Mr. Moore's contribution was mentioned in a press communication which I read on the train one day. I am not criticizing the receipt of that cheque, or suggesting for one moment that it was improper. If Mr. Moore wished to send his old friend a ten dollar bill, he had a perfect right to do so. If my friend sees fit to give me a thousand dollar bill I say he has a perfect right to do so.
Those who have read the life of Disraeli will recall that Mrs. Willyams gave him a thousand pound note which he put away in the pocket of the coat he that day was wearing. He forgot about it for some time, and subsequently discovered it in the pocket of his jacket The contribution itself cannot by any possibility be said to be wrong. If your friend desires to assist you in maintaining your office or securing your return to the House of Commons, he has a perfect right to do so, and I venture to point out that there are very few members in this house, if there are any, who have not at some time in their lives received assistance, probably very small or very trifling, but yet indicative of the spirit of helpfulness and the good will of the individual contributor towards the one whose return to this house is desired. There cannot be anything wrong in that; the law contemplates that it will be so.
During the life of each succeeding parliament an effort has been made to limit, circumscribe and restrict the extent to which contributions should be made, and more than that, the persons who should make them. Perhaps hon. members will recall that between the years 1921 and 1925 this parliament placed upon the statute books a provision whereby contributions by corporations or companies were made illegal, and, that the hon. member from Winnipeg, who has just asked a question, through his activity in the privileges and elections committee was responsible for its recall; it was repealed before the election of 1930 was held. After the election of 1925 and during the succeeding parliament, owing to irregularities which came about in connection with the election of Athabaska, the privileges and elections committee met, and in no sectional or party sense endeavoured to prepare such legislation for submission to this house as would prevent a recurrence of the condition to which reference had been made. The election of 1930 came on with the restriction eliminated as to corporations,

Elections Act-Mr. Bennett
making -contributions. It will ibe recalled a special provision was made in the statute whereby companies were organized-my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) knows what I mean-for the purpose of -making contributions to the -cause of the Progressive or farmers' movement in the western provinces, and funds were collected for that purpose; that is well known. It was discussed in the lifetime of the house eleoted in 1925. I say that to the hon. gentleman for East Hamilton because I suppose, like most new members, he has -the very laudable ambition to accomplish a reform, and I take it, that no member will deny him the -right to achieve that ambition if he can. But I merely take a little time to point out that for -the last half a century successive committees on privileges and elections, not only in Canada, not only in Australia, not only in England, but in every country where democratic government prevails, have -made an effort, first, merely to define what constitutes -improper -practices at elections, and second, to limit the -contributions that may be made by -individuals or corporations to the funds of (a) the party and (b) the individual. In the United States it will be recalled that in connection with the great national campaigns -contributions are now made public and it is stated with particularity by whom they are made. We have such a provision in our Jaw. We have provided that every member of this house shall make a return of -his election expenses -indicating the sources -from which the funds came to pay those expenses, whether from hi-mself or from a contributor. If those who have interest in the matter will go through the returns filed after the last election they will realize that various -people made contributions towards their particular favourite -candidate, sometimes $5, sometimes $25, sometimes $100, sometimes $1,000. But it is within the memory of members of this house that in at least one return with respect to one of the elections held since 1921 the candidate-mark you, he was not successful-showed he had expended over $75,000. No one for a moment said that that money was not -properly expended. There were supporting vouchers, there were the details of the expenditure. It indicated to me, at least, that the ascertaining of the will of the people had become highly expensive for those who endeavoured to speak for a party in the determination of that question.
Now, let us ascertain what other appropriate remedies may be suggested. There may be some difficulty in that regard. In Australia, confronted with similar conditions, they endeavoured to cure the evil -by compulsory

voting. How many members of this house are prepared to say that the enactment of legislation to -make it an offence to fail to vote will cure the evil to which reference has been made?

speechtext:
I believe it would. But, remember, this country is so vast in area and its population so scattered that the difficulty of maintaining successfully a -charge against an elector for not voting is such as to make it wel-l-nigh impossible to secure a conviction, a situation that makes it most difficult to say that that is the remedy to be sought.
Now, it has been the -practice in this -country, as it has been in most democratic countries, to say, and quite properly so, that party contributions made by those who are seeking benefits for the purpose of ensuring the receipt of those benefits is wrong. I have heard no one attempt to justify any other view. But the difficulty always has been to ascertain whether or not you had the sequence -the payment, the expectation, the reward. Those have been the really difficult things to determine. If you show that over a long course of years any individual regardless of such expectations has contributed funds to assist in the election of his party's candidates, that is not indicative of any evil intent. But then you come to the question as old as the Pacific scandal in this -parliament. I wonder if members * sometimes look back upon the journals of the house of the days of the so-called Pacific scandal and realize what progress Canada has made in minimizing what were then regarded as great evils, and if they realize that what in those days was regarded as serious would to-day be regarded as a mere incident. I wonder if that fact is borne in on the minds of hon. members. Re-ad the journals of the house of that day, read the evidence given and compare it with the evidence given last year 'before the Beau-harnois committee, and what is the result? It is for that reason that I suggest the great difficulty that arises in merely saying that something shall go to the committee on privileges and elections where various ideas are thrown into the melting pot and something emerges to be embodied in a statute

Elections Act-Mr. Bennett
which accomplishes no good. That is a fact known to every member of this house who has taken the trouble to study the subject.
I have felt that compulsory voting might accomplish some good.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
It may be I am wrong
as to that. I have inquired of my friends in Australia how in practice compulsory voting has worked out there. I think they have also a similar statute in New Zealand now.
I was told that the law had this effect, that, first, it greatly increased the number of men who voted, and, secondly, it did something to lessen the possibility of improprieties in the conduct of elections.
* Mr. HEAPS:	If the right hon. gentleman
will permit a question-could he inform the house whether they have also compulsory registration in Australia?
Mr.'BENNETT:	I dealt with that in the
irst few words of my observations on the luestion of registration. I am not going1 to develop the idea beyond saying that I think there must be some method of registration and some method of revision, because as the law stands now there are many names of dead men and women on voters' lists that should not be there.
The immediate matter that has given rise to the motion of the hon. member for East Hamilton is the Beauharnois scandal, in connection with which the special committee found that very large sums of money had been paid to a political party. This gives me an opportunity to make just one observation. The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) went to Winnipeg and made a speech, in the course of which he took occasion to say that money had been paid to the representative of the then opposition and returned at my instance.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS

That is what the right
hon. gentleman said at London, not Winnipeg-that money had been paid to the representative of the Conservative party and at my instance returned. I have always felt -I want to do justice to the right hon. gentleman-that it must have been either an error -a very simple one on his part, but not so simple so far as we are concerned-or it must have been done with malice aforethought. I cannot think any good purpose would have been served by his doing it with malice afore-[DOT] thought, because ultimately he must come back to this chamber and meet here his peers
who heard the discussion and read the evidence that dealt with that question. In that evidence it was never suggested by any person that a sum of money had been paid to the federal Conservative party by Beauharnois interests. There is the record and it speaks for itself. Then why should it be said money was so received and returned?

Does^my right
hon. friend say no money was contributed by Beauharnois to any member of the Conservative party, to be paid into the party funds?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
I am now dealing with
the evidence. I say that the right hon. leader of the opposition went to London and made a speech which he either knew was false or he should have known was false, and he therefore was wilfully negligent in the discharge of his duties, for he had the hardihood to say that this sum of money was received and returned at my instance. That was what he said.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext: May I say to my right hon. friend that I made no statement, at London or anywhere else, which I knew was false. I would have made no such statement. If I made an incorrect statement I at once retract it, and I accept my right hon. friend's word as to what is right and what is wrong in the circumstances. What I do say is this: what I am speaking of is the contribution-my right hon. friend has just referred to it-being made by Beauharnois, and all along my understanding has been that Beau-hamois did make a contribution to a member of the Conservative party, which was to have gone into the funds of the Conservative party and would have gone there but for the fact that the present leader of the government indicated that it should not be done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
In the report made the
next day, and in this case prepared from a printed or typewritten manuscript, this is what is said:
As the law stands a corporation or an individual has a perfect right to make a contribution to the funds of a political party, and the party a right in accepting contributions. Some years ago a law was enacted which made contributions from corporations to political parties illegal. I much fear the law was never greatly respected, but it was there. At the session of 1930 that section of the Elections Act was repealed. The repeal was made at the request of Labour members in the House of Commons, the reason being that under the law as it stood it would have been illegal for labour unions or farmers' organizations without incorporation as political bodies to make contributions to the campaign funds of Labour candidates or farmer

Elections Act-Mr. Bennett
candidates. In commenting upon the amounts contributed to the funds of the Liberal party, and accepted, it is desirable that this fact of there being no illegality about the transaction should be fully and clearly understood.
For reasons which I think are apparent I endeavoured to repeat that to the house this evening. Then the right hon. gentleman went on:
The next point to note is that contributions were made by those associated with Beauharnois to both political parties, to the Conservative party and members of the party in the federal field, as well as to the party or members of the party in Ontario and Quebec, and that the return of the contribution made to the general fund of the Conservative party was on grounds of party expediency and not of public policy.
When the general elections came on, Mr. Sweezey made a contribution to the campaign funds of both the Liberal and Conservative parties. Later the contribution given to the treasurer of the Conservative party was returned, he, according to Mr. Sweezey's statement of what he had been told, having had instructions from Mr. Bennett to return the contribution. Now what was Mr. Bennett's reason for directing the return of the amount contributed?
Mark you, it never was contributed, and the evidence shows that to be the case.

That is not what the
hon. gentleman was dealing with.
