speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
Not so far as I know,
and what is more, that is not what the right hon. gentleman was dealing with. The right hon. gentleman went to London and told the people that the contribution was made and returned at my instance because, he said, I believed there would be an inquiry, and it was done for party expediency and not public good. Sir, the person alleged to have made the contribution, without my knowledge, wrote a letter to the public press and denied that any such contribution was made, a few days after that speech. Then why did the right hon. gentleman make that statement in London? Why did he speak of the sums of money having been received and returned, unless for one purpose? Being in the valley of humiliation and unable to extricate himself, he tries to drag down other men to keep him company.
I knew the time would come and the opportunity would arise when I might say to this house that that statement was untrue. The motion of the hon. member for East Hamilton [Mr. Bennett.J
affords that opportunity. Not only that, but with my knowledge or at my instance there was never any money received from Beauharnois. Hon. members will recall that I stated last session that I felt possibly it should have been my duty to go before that committee and make a statement in view of what was said.
It is an unpleasant sort of thing to inquire into this matter further, but I did so, and the language that was used when the offer of a contribution was made, according to the person who received that offer, was, "Not a damned cent." That was the answer; I hesitate to put it to the house in that way, but that is what was said. I do greatly deprecate an unfair statement being made for nothing but a sinister purpose, but I accept the statement of 'the right hon. gentleman. The only difficulty is that my right hon. friend made the statement in London and was content that it should be published broadcast. It does not do much good now to stand in .this house, when he had the knowledge before him at the time he made his speech only a few months ago, and say, "I did not intend that" or "I am sorry, and I accept the hon. gentleman's word." It is not my word; it is what the record shows, what is written there and what he referred to during the progress of his speech. Then why misrepresent it? That is what I want to know, and that is what many people want to know. I knew the time would come when, before a jury of his peers, he would have to face that statement, untrue, highly improper, and calculated to mislead people merely for his own personal advantage.
I point these things out, sir, because the hon. member for East Hamilton has said that during the course of his election much attention was paid to this particular matter, and that it became of considerable importance that he should propose the resolution he now brings forward. In fact, I think he promised his electors he would do so, and as I have said, he has discharged that duty fairly and, for a new member, with very great credit and distinction to himself. But I ask him to consider whether or not any progress will be made by sending this resolution to the committee on privileges and elections. Would it not be advisable to have this matter dealt with when redistribution is dealt with, and when this parliament will frame, as it must frame, a new election act to provide for the forthcoming election, with new lists in new constituencies?

Elections Act-Mr. Bourassa
If it is the sense of this house that the motion should pass and that the matter should be sent to the committee certainly I will not, nor will the government, bring forward any objection to that being done. I have discharged my duty when I point out to the hon. gentleman the conditions to which I have referred and the desirability of considering this matter when perhaps party feelings and passions are less strong and when the members of the committee may be better able to take a dispassionate view of a situation which must be remedied if democracy is to survive, and which must be frankly met if we are to maintain our institutions in their vigour and strength. I have merely put the matter before the hon. member in this way;
I leave it to the house to determine whether or not a good purpose would be served by having the resolution go to the committee on privileges and elections at this time. I repeat frankly that no opposition will be offered by the government to this being done, but I say with equal frankness that I do not think any good purpose will be served by following that course at this time.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
The
right hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) has covered a pretty wide field, more or less directly related to the matter under consideration, but on one point especially I beg respectfully to disagree with his view. He states that the proper time and occasion for the committee to deal with this phase of the electoral system, that is, contribution to party funds, will be when the same committee will have to deal with redistribution.
I was a member of this house, Mr. Speaker, when one redistribution took place, and I kept in close touch with proceedings on a couple of other occasions. My impression is that during those times the committee had its hands full, the whole time being taken up with the question of redistribution only. Surely the right hon. gentleman cannot expect that at the next session the committee will be able to deal with redistribution, with campaign funds, with amendments to the elections act and so on. It would take at least two or three sessions. It seems to me all those things have to be taken seriatim.
I was interested and pleased to hear the hon. gentleman refer to old times both in England and in this country. There is no doubt that the evil of which the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell) spoke is an old one. At this moment I take the opportunity to congratulate the hon. member, both upon his successful campaign and his
maiden speech. No doubt this evil will last for ever, but the same thing can be said of anything connected with human affairs. One of the objects of parliament is to deal with evils as they occur and to correct them as far as possible, with the expectation not of eradicating them altogether but rather of minimizing their effects. The argument advanced by the right hon. gentleman in connection with that aspect of the question is similar to the sceptical criticisms made of the League of Nations because that body has not been able to prevent the present trouble between China and Japan. I do not take that view. We are not all-powerful-not even the right hon. gentleman is all-powerful-but with the cooperation of men of good will in all parties we can accomplish something from time to time.
The question dealt with by this resolution is one that might be better taken up separately. The operation of the elections act, the redistribution and qualification of voters, compulsory voting and so on are all different aspects; they have nothing to do with this matter. This is outside of the electoral law, so to speak.
The question of campaign funds is a very complicated one, and I am not unmindful of the statement made by the Prime Minister that campaign funds in themselves are not wrong. They may be necessary, but I do not believe they are necessary to the extent to which they are functioning in our present system. My firm belief is and my experience has been that a very large proportion of the campaign funds are not used either in corrupting the people or in helping the candidate; they are pocketed by the so-called local leaders. These men come to the committee and say, "You know, in such and such a district I command so many votes; if I had five hundred or a thousand dollars at my disposal I could assure you a majority." Nine times out of ten the money remains in their pockets; they are benefited to that extent but neither the electors, the candidate nor the party have received any good therefrom.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext: How does the hon. gentleman know that?

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE TO PRIVILEGES AND ELECTIONS COMMITTEE OF QUESTION OF ELECTION FUNDS
speechtext:
I know it from experience. As the hon. gentleman has raised the issue, I will give him an example. When I was chosen as a candidate some thirty-eight years ago the first condition which I imposed was that I would not seek any campaign funds from any electoral committee. That was the condition I laid down to my electors and to my late revered leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He gladly

Elections Act-Mr. Bourassa
accepted that condition, because in those days the Liberal party was mighty poor and Sir Wilfrid had a peculiar tenderness for any candidate who did not ask for any financial assistance from his party. My second election was more of a contest and two of my friends, both good fellows and very honest, thought fit to go to the committee to Montreal and ask for a subscription. They got that subscription and they returned to a certain corner in my constituency where one of them spent all of his share while the other one kept a little reward for himself. When I found out what had happened I borrowed money from the bank and I reimbursed the treasurer of the Liberal party. I was thus enabled to continue to speak and vote just as freely in that parliament as I had during the previous parliament. At the next election I decided to make an experiment. I visited this same comer of my constituency and the local leaders came to me and in a mysterious manner asked if Mr. So-and-So would be there. I told them that he would not, and they then wanted to know who would come. I told them no one would come, and then they inquired as to what they would do for an organization. I have no scruples in admitting that I have usually spent a little money here and there. There might be a poor devil of a settler living twenty miles from the polling booth and having no rig in which to come to the village, and I have helped him out and given the man who brought him to vote two or three dollars. It may have been against the letter of the law, but I do not deny having done it. These poor fellows have no other pleasure in life than to come in and vote once in five yearn. However, there was no committee, no place where the wiseacres of the village could get together and get drunk on whiskey and beer and then cry out, "Hurrah for the Liberal party." On this particular occasion, in 'carrying out my experiment, I spent not one single cent in that particular district, and I obtained the same number of votes as I had received at the previous election. This convinced me that the so-called necessity for campaign funds is to a large extent caused by the exactions of canvassers of local leaders who pocket most of the money they receive. So much for that aspect of the case.
There is still a broader aspect, the source of these subscriptions. The right hon. gentleman has mentioned various amendments to the law, so I will not refer to any detail. It seems to me a distinction should be drawn between corporations and individuals who have no direct dealings with the government but who may have a personal or a public interest in supporting one party or the other,

or one candidate or the other, and those who are directly interested in getting favours from the state. What I have always objected to is the contribution which is made, generally to both parties, such as the contributions made in the past by the railroad companies or by tlie Canadian Manufacturers Association, which has always had a permanent and enormous interest at stake.
I have previously referred to the elections of 1896 which were carried on by the Liberal party in the name of free trade. The curse of protection was to be eradicated for all time; but everyone knows what happened later on-the Hon. Mr. Fielding brought in a moderately protective tariff. I regarded myself as a moderate protectionist. In spite of the great convention of 1893, in spite of the program initiated by my party, I could not believe that free trade could be established in this country, and I so stated in my constituency, to the great scandal of some of my Liberal friends. Afterwards, and upon inquiry, I was informed by one of the most influential ministers that they had engagements. I asked what those engagements were and he replied, "You know, when election time came we needed money, as elections are not won with prayers; we received a subscription from the manufacturers association and we promised them the tariff would not be dealt with too harshly." That shows the effect of campaign funds when contributed by certain corporations. To my mind the contributions which have been made by the manufacturers association from year to year since 1879 have been far more detrimental to the morals of this country and to the independence of this parliament than have the contributions made by Mr. Sweezey and his associates. My feeling is that too much noise has been made over the Beauharnois affair. Of course it is a scandal, but no more than many other things. The right hon. gentleman has properly said: if you look up the records of parliament at the time of the Pacific scandal, you will be amazed to see that things which were considered abominable in those days would probably be accepted as-well, unimportant in these days. What was important in the Pacific scandal? It was not the amount of money contributed. It was the direct connection between Sir George Etienne Cartier and Sir John A. Macdonald as party leaders, and Sir Hugh Allan on the other side. It was the direct, shall I say, conspiracy between the two leaders of the government, two most eminent men, and the man who was interested in procuring the charter and privileges of the company. When you read those letters of

Elections Act-Mr. Bourassa
Sir George Etienne Cartier to this and that man saying-well, I translate it in popular language-put the screw on you for a little more money, that was the scandalous part of it. It was not the amount of money; it was not the secret understandings; it was the brutal fact that the leaders of the government, the leaders of the country, got into direct connection with the organizers of a big railway company which was after privileges from parliament, and secured money from that company on the eve of the session which was to give them their privileges. That was the scandalous part of it.
I quite agree with the hon. member for East Hamilton that the traffic in titles which has been going on in England for a number of years in order to fatten the subscription fund of the Liberal party especially is not so scandalous as some may consider it. My point of view-and I suppose it is the point of view of the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. Spotton)-is that it has been very helpful in one way; it has shown the baseness of many things that were considered very respectable in England some years ago. It has shown what lordships amount to.
Reference has been made at various times to traffic in Senate seats. I well remember one day when Sir Wilfrid Laurier told me his propaganda fund was empty, but that before long perhaps two or three seats could be disposed of in the Senate, and therefore the flow might come again. Of course all those things are known. We might just as well make no bones about them, and not be hypocritical. I believe no reform can be accomplished by cant and hypocrisy. Let us put situations as they are. Human beings being what they are, you cannot cure all those things at once, but I think from time to time efforts could be made to prevent the evils from becoming too great. You have a certain piece of machinery. It gets dirty. You clean it, although you know it will be dirty again five years hence. But you do not say: the chief officer is busy elsewhere, or the chief mechanical engineer is busy; let us wait for a few years from now when there will be a general review of the whole management of the firm and we shall take up the question of the reorganization of the whole machine, therefore let this piece of machinery continue clogging. No; we might just as well cure evils as they come. Supposing the committee should accomplish no great object, I believe it would advance parliament; it would give satisfaction to public opinion if, the motion of the hon. member being accepted, the committee on privileges and elections modestly 41761-10
and effectively would deal with some of these matters and report to the house.
The right hon. gentleman is afraid of some extraordinary bill being introduced that might make the remedy worse than the evil. The right hon. gentleman will still be in power.
I do not believe at the end of the session he will be less powerful or more timid than he has shown himself heretofore, and if there be in what is proposed by the committee anything which the right hon. gentleman in his capacity as Prime Minister and his responsibility as leader of the house thinks improper, it will be open to him to tell us that the proposals of the committee are inacceptable or impracticable. But I really think something could be done on those two things. First, is it possible to control to a certain extent the source of campaign funds? I shall not talk of shutting it out altogether. That is like prohibition. I do not want to draw a red herring across the trail, but we know what prohibition has shown itself to be in practice in all the provinces of Canada that have adopted and tried it, as well as in the United States, in Scandinavia and in Russia. I know, however, something can be and has been done to enhance the cause of temperance and diminish the evil of the liquor traffic. Likewise this country could and should do something in this matter.
I quite agree with the Prime Minister that there is some risk of the Beauharnois affair again cropping up and of party feeling existing in the committee. But party feeling will always exist in the house; party feeling will always exist in every committee of the house. The moment you touch on some question which is directly or indirectly connected with the election of members of parliament, willy-nilly party feeling will run amuck. Next year the question of redistribution will come up. Surely the right hon. gentleman is not so naive as to 'think that either his friends or the friends of the leader of the opposition will have no thought of party success when they come to the question of redistribution of seats. Therefore, if you connect this matter up with the redistribution of seats next year, you will have a double dose of party feeling; whereas, at the present time, the right hon. gentleman to my right being where he is, the right hon. gentleman opposite being where he is, his friends in Toronto being where they are, and the friends of the Liberal party in Quebec being where they are, I believe there is some chance, not of party feeling not arising in the committee, but of the politicians in that committee not showing their party spirit so much this year as next.



Elections Act-Mr. Bourassa
So far as that is concerned, I agree with the leader of the Liberal party that going down into the valley of humiliation is good for parties at times. It gives them strength. First, it purifies them. It did good to the hon. gentlemen on the opposite side to go into opposition once in a while. I have known times when the Conservative party at the height of power has not been exactly a model of public or private virtue. I have known occasions when it would have been rather difficult for the leaders of the Conservative party to pose -well, they could have posed as the Pharisee did, but they could not have made the speech of the Pharisee because the Pharisee was a pretty detestable individual, although nothing appears in the gospel that what he said was not true except that he was a Ettle too proud. But I have known times when the Conservative party oould not have boasted of their virtues or been proud of their vices. Therefore, going into the valley of humiliation at times is good for all parties and all public men. I really believe this session is the one at which we should deal with this aspect of the question. So I think the house should accept the resolution in the good spirit in which it has been presented by the hon. member for Bast Hamilton and for which on my part I thank him heartily.

Mr. St-PERE: Oh!

I can imagine, however, that if certain amendments were put into the election act which would make it a crime to overcharge for a hall during the time of an election, and which would make it a crime for a newspaper to overcharge for space during an election, we might considerably cut down that $25,000. There are 174 miles of the boundary yet to be surveyed and determined, but this is through an uninhabited and unproductive country, and the provincial governments interested desire that 'the boundary which has been so far surveyed should be determined, leaving to a future date the survey of that great waste district.

Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Boards of Trade Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill amending the Boards of Trade Act has in view preventing persons or organizations from using the names "board of trade" or "chamber of commerce" in a district where 'there is a duly constituted board of trade or chamber of commerce, without giving the existing board of trade an

opportunity to present reasons against the incorporation of the second organization in that district, if it is desired so to do.
The first request made to the department of the Secretary of State for this change came from the Toronto Board of Trade, Which has been organized as suoh and has carried on as a board of trade since 1845. An organization advertising itself as the Bloor-Bathurst Board of Trade assumed the functions of a regular board of trade in the district in which the Toronto Board of Trade was operating. The Toronto Board of Trade objected to the operation of this organization on three grounds: First, that it had no authority for styling itself a board of trade; second, that it was not a representative institution, and third, that its existence created confusion in the public mind, and was misleading.
This request of the Toronto Board of Trade for an amendment to the statute was supported by the Ontario Associated Boards of Trade, by chambers of commerce throughout Canada, and also by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and came before 'the department of the Secretary of State for the first time more than a year ago. Finally the following resolution was adopted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce at its last general convention:
Resolved that: The Canadian Chamber of Commerce petition the Dominion government to amend the Boards of Trade Act, chapter 19, R.S.C., 1927, to provide that no person or persons shall use the name "Board of Trade" or "Chamber of Commerce" unless incorporated as such under the provisions of the Boards of Trade Act or of any special act of parliament; and that before granting an application for incorporation, the Secretary of State shall afford any existing boards or chambers in the district affected, an opportunity of showing cause why such incorporation should not be allowed, and providing a suitable penalty for the unauthorized use of such name.
It seemed to me that this request was reasonable, that before a second board of trade in the same district should be incorporated by any statute under the supervision of the Secretary of State, the minister should necessarily give the existing 'board of trade an opportunity to make representations as to whether a second board of trade or chamber of commerce should be incorporated. This bill has that purpose in view, so that if the bill is enacted, in cases where a district is already occupied by an incorporated board of trade, no part of that district could be occupied by any other board of trade which might apply for incorporation without an opportunity being afforded to the existing board to show cause why the proposed change should not be made.

Boards of Trade Act
The Boards of Trade Act also mentions the Dominion Board of Trade, which was incorporated in 1873 and which, for a number of years, functioned as a dominion board of trade. For many years, however, the Dominion Board of Trade has ceased to exist, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, which was incorporated in 1929, has been fulfilling the same functions. Various boards of trade throughout Canada have asked that the act be so amended that -any board of trade may become affiliated with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce for the same purposes for which, in times past, they became affiliated with the Dominion Board of Trade, which is no longer in existence.
Another section of the act provides forcer-tain returns to foe filed with the Secretary of State, containing certain details. At the present time the aot requires that this return shall be signed fey the president and secretary, duly verified by their affidavits. That is a provision of the statute of very long standing, and it is sometimes difficult to have these details verified properly. I suggest that hereafter the signature of the secretary of the board of trade to these returns, without an affidavit, is quite sufficient to satisfy all public purposes.
They may.

Under this
bill they have not that privilege.

Should this bill pass, the
existing board of trade would be afforded an opportunity to show cause against the proposed change and the certificate for the new board would be recorded only with the sanction and authority of the governor in council.

Do I understand that under the provisions of this bill the new board would have to ask for the sanction of parliament whereas under the old legislation it was sufficient to obtain a certificate from the governor in council?

-unless they are incorporated as a body corporate and politic under this act or under a special act of the parliament of Canada.
I intended to insert "under a general or special aot of the parliament of Canada." I am advised that the chamber of commerce and the board of trade in Montreal both are constituted under dominion acts.

If an organization in any
village desires to assume the functions of a board of trade it should be incorporated under the Boards of Trade Act.

As I understand it, if there
was such an organization as the Eastern Townships Board of Trade, the town of Stanstead could not incorporate its board of trade without first consulting the other body and then obtaining a certificate from the governor in council.

The Boards of Trade Act
is administered by the Secretary of State, and if a second board of trade in a particular district desired to be incorporated and applied for incorporation, the officials of the department would notify the existing board which would be afforded an opportunity to show cause against recording the proposed cer-i tificate. After having shown cause, the certificate instead of being recorded at the option of the Secretary of State, as under the existing law, would be recorded only with the sanction and authority of the governor in council. Those are the provisions of section 6 of the act which are incorporated into section 2 of this bill. The bill provides that the words "board of trade" or "chamber of commerce" shall not be used by another body which has not had such a certificate recorded. Chambers of commerce (throughout the country object to other chambers being organized in their respective districts.

Subsection (2) of section 1
says:
No person shall within any district in which there is a duly constituted board, use the words "board of trade," or "chamber of commerce," as part of the name under which they are incorporated or doing business, or any other words so similar as to be liable to be confused therewith, unless they are incorporated as a body corporate and politic under this act or under a special act of the parliament of Canada.
That means that hereafter they cannot simply mil themselves the board of trade. They must be incorporated under the Boards of Trade Act.

In every
small village where there are half a dozen business men who wish to set up a board' of trade, they will! now have to register.

Why should they not? There is no expense to it. It is purely a matter of form in sending in a certificate and becoming registered, after which they are under some supervision, very slight, and they have to make returns from time to time. This is to prevent people from using the name "Board of Trade" for Montreal or for some other town or village for purposes other than those for which boards of trade are constituted; for instance, using the name "Board of Trade" for the purpose of smuggling liquor or entering into other illegal practices.

With deference, I submit to the Secretary of State that the amendment suggested does not meet the evil that he is trying to remedy. What is suggested by the amendment is that provided there is what is called a duly constituted board within a district, then another body of persons cannot use the name without being incorporated.
That is the second section.

That is the section we are at now. Subsection 2 which it is proposed to add to section 3 of the Boards of Trade Act reads:
No person shall-
It does not say: "shall use the words 'board of trade' or 'chamber of commerce' without being duly incorporated under this act," but shall use those words if there is some other duly constituted board within the district, which is quite a different thing.

Boards of Trade Act

My 'hon. friend is not quoting the section. In section 1 of this bill, subsection 2 reads:
No person shall within any district in which there is a duly constituted board, use the words "Board of Trade" or "Chamber of Commerce" as part of the name under which they are incorporated or doing business or any other words so similar as to be liable to be confused therewith, unless they are incorporated-
And so forth. My first provision is that they must be incorporated.

No. That brings up the
point, if my hon. friend will permit me: they must be incorporated before they can use the term, provided there is another duly constituted board within the district. The section does not say "shall not use the words 'board of trade' or 'chamber of commerce' if there is no other board there," so that the evil which the Secretary of State is endeavouring to eliminate is not quite met by this amendment. I can imagine a judicial district in which there is no board of trade at all, and a group of persons being formed for the purposes which my hon. friend suggests, who are not hit in any way by this amendment. That is my point.

As I have already informed the hon. member for West Edmonton, I have not gone so far as to say that no persons shall call themselves by the name of "Board of Trade" unless incorporated. I am going simply this far, that where there is an incorporated board of trade, no other body shall set itself up and call itself a board of trade unless it is incorporated; and second, that when an application is made for incorporation, it will be the duty of the Secretary of State or the officials of his department to notify the existing board of that application, allow them to show cause against the granting of the certificate, and then, if the certificate is granted, it can be granted only with the approval of the governor in council.

I am submitting to my
hon. friend that there is a real evil in the practice here suggested of people using the term "board of trade" for improper purposes, but I am saying that evil has not been eliminated by providing that nobody at all shall use the term "board of trade" without being registered. I suggest that difficulty has not been met by this section.
That brings me to the second point. If my hon. friend is endeavouring, as I agree he is, to prevent competition, let us say between an incorporated board of trade and an unincorporated body, then I think my hon. friend, on looking at the drafting of the section, will agree that it ought to be changed. In the first place the use of the term "duly constituted board" does not mean anything under the statute.

I think this section would mean that if there were a board of trade in a district, you could not have another board of trade in that district without its being incorporated. My hon. friend knows judicial districts cover a pretty large territory.

My hon. friend has just
stated that all boards of trade should be incorporated.

If my hon. friend wishes to accomplish that object, he has not gone that far, I did not say that all boards of trade should be incorporated. The minister could insert a clause which would render punishable with a fine persons who are using the name for wrongful purposes. There are very few men who would know the provisions in regard to incorporation and it is imposing a little too much hardship on people to require them to go through this formality. I am thinking of a judicial district in which there are two, three or four towns, where if you had a board of trade in one town, there could be no board of trade in any other.
Boards of Trade Act
Did the hon. member look at the section with regard to interpretation?

Yes. It means any
judicial district or any town or village. The moment you use the word "district," if you have a board of trade in a judicial district, then you have that district preempted by that one board of trade. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth has put forward the views that I wish to express.
